name: Grunth
summary: In Orgrimmar, Grunth eagerly seeks the company of Horde champions. He lives in the Drag orphanage and, during Children's Week, travels across Kalimdor and the Eastern Kingdoms to learn what makes a hero.

sections.title: A Curious Child of the Horde
sections.body: Grunth is a young orc orphan in Orgrimmar's Drag, cared for by Orphan Matron Battlewail. Raised in Durotar's harsh red wastes, he watches armored adventurers with awe and asks them question after question. Are armored warriors truly terrifying? Why doesn't lightning on water kill every fish? Will he ever see someone fight a real dragon?

sections.title: Children's Week Journeys
sections.body: During Children's Week, an Orcish Orphan Whistle calls Grunth to travel with adventurers across the world. He hopes to meet High Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof in Mulgore and see Lordaeron's ruined throne room. He also wants to visit the rugged frontiers where his people fight for their future.

faq.answer: Grunth is an orc child living at the orphanage in the Drag of Orgrimmar. Orphan Matron Battlewail cares for him, and he dreams of becoming a legendary hero of the Horde.
Grunth lives with the other orphans in Orgrimmar's Drag. During Children's Week, Orphan Matron Battlewail can summon him anywhere with an Orcish Orphan Whistle.

faq.q: What places does Grunth want to visit?
faq.answer: Grunth wants to visit great places and figures of the Horde. He asks to see High Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof in Thunder Bluff, the Ratchet docks, and Lordaeron's ruined throne room.

faq.q: What kind of personality does Grunth have?
faq.answer: Grunth is loud, curious, and full of imagination. He asks adventurers strange questions, like what “zug zug” means and whether a wingless fly is called a walk. He even mentions shoving a rock up his nose.

angles.text: As a Horde champion, guiding Grunth during Children's Week shows you a generation born free of demonic servitude, and what your faction strives to protect.
As an orc, Grunth reflects Durotar's youth, raised with tribal honor and the demands of survival, far from the dark lethargy of the internment camps.
